newsitem.title: ITALY: Aeroporti di Roma foresees rising profits.
newsitem.headline: Aeroporti di Roma foresees rising profits.

text.p: Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), making its stock market debut later this month, expects to see increased profitability with business continuing to grow in coming years.
"This year's (net) profit will not be less than that of 1996 and there will be continued growth in successive years," ADR managing director Gaetano Galia told a news conference.

Aeroporti di Roma boosted its net profits by 61 percent in 1996 to 90.2 billion lire and increased its turnover 11 percent to 1.16 trillion lire. Gross operating margin was up 20 percent to 282.5 billion lire.

Galia said, however, that in the short term operating margins would be held down by the cost of the company's ongoing multi-year reorganisation and development plan. Some 30 billion lire was already earmarked for this in 1997.
Gross operating margin this year and the next will not increase, "but we guarantee it will start rising again from 1999," Galia said.
He said ADR's bourse listing later this month after a public sale offer was both "a goal and a starting point" for the future.
From the year 2000 onwards, ADR officials said the aim was to increase return on sales by over 50 percent.

In 1996, some 34 percent of ADR's turnover came from handling at its two airports at Fiumicino and Ciampino, with 22 percent from commercial activities, 16.4 percent from landing and takeoff charges and 13.1 percent from catering.

This mix is set to change in the future, Galia said, with more emphasis on commercial revenues and added-value business. In the last three years commercial turnover, at 255 billion lire in 1996, had grown at around 10 percent a year.

Galia said passenger traffic was likely to continue to grow at a rate above the European average and was already up 9.3 percent in the first half of this year against the same 1996 period, pointing up the importance of Rome as a major European hub especially towards the south and east.

Aeroporti di Roma, 73.58 percent owned by state industrial holding IRI, is putting a minimum 41 percent stake of the company's capital on the market which can be upped to 45 percent in the case of extra demand.

Of the offer of 49.2 million ordinary shares, at least 30 percent will be offered to the public, five percent will be reserved for company employees, and 65 percent will be left for Italian and foreign institutional investors.
